title: Multi-LLM Adaptive Conformal Inference for Reliable LLM Response
claim: Prior filtering methods either discard too many true claims or lose coverage; ours keeps both high coverage and high retention.
layout: 3 side-by-side panels, left-to-right, struck-through text and coverage/retention labels below
description: Three columns compare the same LLM-generated medical paragraph about amitriptyline and alprazolam, with each claim tagged [T] or [F]. The left column, BCI (Mohri and Hashimoto et al.), strikes through nearly every sentence, and the false claims are in red. Below it: Target Coverage High, Retention Low. The middle column, CCI (Cherian et al.), strikes through nothing, so the false claims stay visible in red. Below it: Target Coverage Not Enough, Retention High. The right column, MACI (Ours), strikes through only the false claims. Below it: Target Coverage High, Retention High. Headers are bold serif titles with citations. Red text marks false claims. The eye goes first to the heavy strikethrough on the left, then to the summary labels at the bottom of each column.
caption: Comparison of Conformal Inference Methods. T (true) and F (false) denote ground-truth labels per claim. Basic Conformal Inference [ref] attains coverage by aggressive filtering, yielding low retention. Conditional Conformal Inference [ref] proposes adaptive thresholds but relaxes guarantees; MACI achieves both high coverage and retention.
abstract: Ensuring factuality is essential for the safe use of Large Language Models (LLMs) in high-stakes domains such as medicine and law. Conformal inference provides distribution-free guarantees, but existing approaches are either overly conservative, discarding many true-claims, or rely on adaptive error rates and simple linear models that fail to capture complex group structures. To address these challenges, we reformulate conformal inference in a multiplicative filtering setting, modeling factuality as a product of claim-level scores. Our method, Multi-LLM Adaptive Conformal Inference (MACI), leverages ensembles to produce more accurate factuality-scores, which in our experiments led to higher retention, while validity is preserved through group-conditional calibration. Experiments show that MACI consistently achieves user-specified coverage with substantially higher retention and lower time cost than baselines. Our repository is available at https://github.com/MLAI-Yonsei/MACI
